items.title: Improving Solid-State Battery Safety and Performance Through Advanced Transfer Printing
items.summary:
Solid-state batteries use solid-based electrolytes instead of liquid electrolytes, offering the potential to reduce fire risks and increase energy density. To achieve high energy density, the solid electrolyte must be thinner than 20 micrometers (µm) while maintaining uniform thickness over a large area. [...] AZoM
An AZoNetwork Site

# Improving Solid-State Battery Safety and Performance Through Advanced Transfer Printing

A Korean research team has developed a transfer printing process that enables solid electrolytes, a key component of solid-state batteries, to be fabricated as very thin, uniform, and defect-free layers over large areas. The technology is expected to provide a foundation for the large-area manufacturing of high-energy-density solid-state batteries. [...] A research team led by Principal Researcher Yongku Kang and Senior Researcher Myung-Soo Park at the Korea Research Institute of Chemical Technology (KRICT, President Seokmin Shin) developed a transfer printing technology using the garnet-type oxide solid electrolyte LLZTO, in which a solid electrolyte layer is first fabricated on a separate substrate and then transferred onto an electrode.

items.title: Chemical Breakthrough Could Unlock the “Holy Grail” of Solid-State Battery Technology
items.summary:
Solid-state batteries are a promising alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries because they replace flammable liquid electrolytes with solid materials. Credit: Stock

### A simple chemical treatment could overcome a persistent weakness in next-generation solid-state batteries. [...] Scientists in China have developed a thin protective coating that could help overcome a major obstacle to longer-lasting, high-capacity batteries. In laboratory tests, solid-state batteries using the treated lithium metal retained 82.3% of their initial capacity after 300 charging cycles, compared with just 43.0% for batteries using untreated lithium. [...] This illustration depicts the in-situ formation of the PFSIn-Li interlayer on a lithium metal anode. A liquid precursor containing a fluorinated siloxane polymer and indium salt reacts on the lithium surface to generate a multifunctional hybrid film. The organic polymer network interpenetrates with inorganic lithium fluoride, lithium-indium alloy, and lithium silicon oxide nanodomains, simultaneously suppressing dendrite growth and stabilizing the interface with the sulfide solid electrolyte.

items.title: EV Battery Executive Shares An Uncomfortable Truth About Solid-State Batteries
items.summary:
Share

Comment

Solid-state batteries will likely be commercialized at a larger scale in non-automotive applications before widespread electric vehicle adoption, Korean battery giant LG Energy Solution said during a media roundtable with reporters at its newly opened Lansing, Michigan, battery plant last week. [...] You’re probably exhausted from reading all about solid-state battery-powered EVs that sound like they’re about to hit the market but never do. But all the investment and research behind the technology from startups and established players is real. Battery scientists believe solid-state cells can unlock substantially more driving range, improve the cells’ thermal profiles to eliminate fire risks, and charge at blistering speeds. [...] However, LGES echoed the concerns around its mass manufacturing, saying progress has yet to happen on that front. “The problem with solid state is large-scale production,” Robert Lee, North America president for LGES said. “It has very good energy density, so if you're making a small form factor, you should be able to get there. If you’re making very large form factors, most companies are struggling,” he added.

items.title: Solid-state coolers run 10% colder when current flows with a graded Seebeck coefficient | EurekAlert!
items.summary:
Portable coolers that keep insulin cold on a trip, mini refrigerators in cars, and the lasers inside fiber-optic networks all rely on solid-state cooling — no moving parts, no refrigerant gases, just electric current pumping heat. A study in The Innovation reports a way to make such a cooler run colder without inventing a new material: grade the Seebeck coefficient — the property that sets how much heat each electron carries — from one end of the material to the other. [...] EurekAlert! Science News

Tongji University–led team grades the Seebeck coefficient inside n-type Bi2Te2.7Se0.3, making cooling depend on current direction and adding a new design degree of freedom
